item.research_question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the phonon heat conductivity and vibrational density of states in the refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr?
item.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr (equiatomic quinary refractory high-entropy alloy, bcc structure)
item.processing_route: Preparation of random bcc samples (128,000 atoms, 13.5 nm edge) followed by Metropolis Monte Carlo evolution with Kawasaki-type swaps (10 swaps per step, 100 K rejection temperature) for up to 4.7e6 steps to induce SRO; thermal conductivity calculated via non-equilibrium molecular dynamics at 300 K.
item.test_conditions: Temperature: 300 K (target); Monte Carlo temperature: 100 K; Simulation time for NEMD: 0.6 ns for gradient application, 0.4 ns for property calculation; Heat flux induced by thermostats at 0.8 T and 1.2 T.
key_findings: SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12% compared to the random alloy.
The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys (HfTi, TiZr).
Phonon density of states shows depletion of modes around 6 THz and population of modes at 7 THz due to SRO.
The highest peak of the optical band at around 7 THz starts to show up with the onset of SRO.
The high-frequency part of the VDOS (6–8 THz) is populated mostly by Ti atoms, and to a lesser degree by Zr and Hf.
A percolation threshold is observed slightly before 1e5 MC steps, marked by a jump in the volume fraction of the largest cluster.
The Fisher exponent for cluster size distribution reaches τ = 2.19 after the percolation threshold, consistent with bcc lattice site percolation.
SRO reduces the width of the pair correlation function peaks from 0.025 nm (random) to 0.022 nm (SRO).
item.mechanism: The authors argue that while phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce thermal conductivity, the increase in conductivity is due to the formation of SRO cluster percolation pathways (specifically HfTi and TiZr B2 structures) that facilitate heat transport, alongside a modification of the high-frequency phonon density of states that reduces scattering.
item.limitations: The study focuses on 'perfect' bulk crystals without defects; the EAM potential used is validated at low temperatures but its applicability at high temperatures (above 800 K) requires further study; the analysis is limited to a specific bcc refractory HEA.
item.future_work: Further studies beyond the scope of this work would be required to assess the applicability at high temperatures of the EAM potential used here.
quotes: SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %.
The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys.
Due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity.

item.research_question: How does the evolution of chemical short-range order (SRO) and the formation of ordered clusters affect the lattice thermal conductivity of a refractory high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations combined with Monte Carlo (MC) Kawasaki exchange process; samples evolved from random to SRO over up to 4.7 million MC steps at 300 K.
item.test_conditions: Temperature of 300 K for primary analysis; additional calculations at 1000 K and 1300 K; simulation time scale near 1 ns.
key_findings: Thermal conductivity increases by 12% for the case of maximum SRO (after 4.7 million MC steps) compared to the random alloy.
The random alloy has a thermal conductivity of 0.765 W/(Km), while the SRO alloy reaches 0.86 W/(Km).
The increase in heat conductivity is small when only small ordered clusters are present (≤ 10^4 MC steps) but increases more strongly when large or percolating clusters form (≥ 10^5 MC steps).
SRO leads to a 12.5% reduction of atomic displacements due to the formation of ordered phases.
The cluster size distribution follows a power law with a Fisher exponent τ = 2.19.
The fractal dimension of the cluster structure is around 2.4 at the percolation transition and less than 2 at the end of simulations.
Conductivity does not decrease significantly with temperature (less than 7% decrease from 300 K to 1300 K) for either random or SRO samples.
The mixed model with a coefficient β = 0.65 accurately describes the simulated heat conductivities as a function of the volume fraction of the random phase.
item.mechanism: The increase in thermal conductivity is explained by a composite model where the material consists of a random HEA matrix and various ordered B2 phases (HfNb, HfTi, TiZr, Ta clusters) which have higher thermal conductivity than the matrix. The formation of these ordered phases reduces lattice distortion (atomic displacements) and alters the vibrational density of states (VDOS) by introducing structure in the high-frequency part of the spectrum, rather than changing elastic constants.
item.limitations: The simulation results at high temperatures might be considered results only for a model single-phase bcc HEA, as experiments show a fraction of hcp phase at high temperatures (transition temperature around 800 K). The interatomic potential used provides excellent agreement with ab-initio elastic constants but may not fully capture all SRO evolution details without further validation. Analytical models like Slack and Cahill fail to predict the increase in conductivity due to SRO.
item.future_work: Future studies require improved potential development, including machine learning potentials, to model SRO evolution and its effect on different properties. Additional studies are needed to ascertain the appropriate description of SRO evolution at room temperature. The net outcome of SRO on radiation resistance (balancing increased conductivity against defect trapping) needs detailed study.
quotes: The increase can be quantitatively explained by a simple composite model, where the material is assumed to be a combination of several phases, each with different heat conductivity.
